::: notes
0:00–0:45. This chart is the thesis in one image: six production trading services, ranked by technical debt priority, computed entirely from operational records. No source code was read to produce it. The next 15 minutes explain why that matters, how it was built, and why you can trust it.

## The problem lives outside the code

<span class="tag">MOTIVATION</span>

- In vendor-dominated trading IT, source code is **inaccessible**, so the dominant measurement tools (SonarQube, SQALE, CAST) are structurally inapplicable
- The debt that matters here sits in **infrastructure lifecycle exposure, patch delay and operational instability**, which code-centric tools cannot observe
- The consequences are measurable and compound:
  - <span class="n">10%</span> more technical debt → <span class="n n-hot">−16%</span> gross return on assets in COTS platforms [@bankerTechnicalDebtFirm2020]
  - one month of patch delay → <span class="n n-hot">4.9×</span> higher odds of compromise; three months → <span class="n n-hot">9.1×</span> [@tizioSoftwareUpdatesStrategies2023]
  - repaying architectural debt cut incidents by <span class="n n-cool">84%</span> in production microservices [@detoledoReducingIncidentsMicroservices2021]

<div class="takeaway">The costliest debt in this environment is invisible to the standard tools, but its symptoms are recorded daily in ITSM and CMDB systems.</div>

::: notes
0:45–2:00. Frame the environment: continuous availability, FINMA oversight, vendor platforms that cannot be refactored. Then the three anchor numbers, delivered slowly. The last line sets up the whole design: the symptoms are already being recorded, we just need an instrument that reads them.
:::

## The gap and the research questions

<span class="tag">RQ · CHAPTER 1–2</span>

Across 44 primary studies on TD prioritisation, quantitative multi-criteria approaches are uncommon and industrial validation is rare [@lenarduzziSystematicLiteratureReview2021]. **No reviewed study combines** service-level indicators, multi-criteria prioritisation, live operational data and a trading IT context.

<div style="margin-top:0.7em">
<div class="qa"><div class="q" style="font-weight:700">RQ1</div><div class="a">How can technical debt in mission-critical trading systems be prioritised quantitatively at the service level using operational data?</div></div>
<div class="qa"><div class="q" style="font-weight:700">RQ2</div><div class="a">To what extent do operational service management metrics serve as valid proxies for technical debt severity?</div></div>
<div class="qa"><div class="q" style="font-weight:700">RQ3</div><div class="a">How stable are the resulting rankings when criterion weights are perturbed?</div></div>
</div>

::: notes
2:00–3:00. Emphasise the four-way combination: each pairwise element exists in the literature, the combination does not. RQ2 is deliberately worded as "to what extent": the proxy link is treated as a testable hypothesis throughout, not a premise. That framing recurs on the evaluation slides.
:::

## Design: five indicators, one auditable instrument

<span class="tag">METHOD · DSR</span>

Design Science Research [@hevnerDesignScienceInformation2004]; single-organisation embedded case study; unit of analysis = the IT service as a configuration item.

| Indicator | Source | Debt dimension (Table 2.3) |
|---|---|---|
| Incident frequency | ITSM | Architectural |
| Mean time to restore (MTTR) | ITSM | Infrastructure / platform |
| Change failure rate (CFR) | ITSM | Process |
| Patch recency | CMDB | Vulnerability |
| Unsupported component months | CMDB | Infrastructure lifecycle |

<p class="small muted" style="margin-top:0.5em">Dimension assignments are this study's literature-grounded synthesis. Documentation, test coverage and coupling indicators were excluded on data availability, not relevance.</p>

::: notes
3:00–4:15. Walk one row fully (MTTR: Forsgren et al. validate the metric, Nord et al. ground its diagnostic reading as debt impeding recovery from change). State the exclusions and why: honesty about what could not be measured is part of the audit trail. Pre-empts "why these five?".
:::

## From records to ranking

<span class="tag">METHOD · TOPSIS</span>

<div class="cols">
<div>
**Pipeline**

1. Extract indicators from live ITSM/CMDB records
2. Vector normalisation (preserves extreme observations)
3. Weighting: equal <span class="n">(0.20 each)</span> and differential <span class="n">(0.30 MTTR & patch recency)</span>
4. TOPSIS closeness coefficient <span class="n">C<sub>i</sub> ∈ [0, 1]</span>
5. Rank: lowest C<sub>i</sub> = highest debt priority
</div>
<div>
**Why TOPSIS**

- Handles mixed cost/benefit criteria and different scales in one procedure
- Produces a full ranking, unlike VIKOR's compromise set or AHP alone
- Precedent: @albarakManagingTechnicalDebt2022 for TD, but on controlled data
- Method choice treated as a **robustness question**, tested against SAW and VIKOR
</div>
</div>

::: notes
4:15–5:15. Keep this brisk; examiners know TOPSIS. The two points to land: differential weights are a declared practitioner assumption, not literature-derived, and are themselves stress-tested; and method choice is not defended a priori but empirically, which is where the interesting findings come from.
:::

## The data, and its honest limits

<span class="tag">DATA · CHAPTER 4</span>

<div class="cols">
<div>
- Portfolio of <span class="n">108</span> services; <span class="n">53</span> small vendor GUIs excluded; <span class="n">6</span> selected for demonstration on **data completeness** over the full window
- <span class="n">Jan 2024 – Dec 2025</span>, production records only, anonymised at source
- Quality filters: alarm-storm consolidation, <span class="n">&lt;0.1 h</span> auto-closures removed, <span class="n">98th percentile</span> MTTR cap
</div>
<div>
**Declared limitations**

- Recording practices vary by team → scores are **ordinal signals**, not measurements
- CFR shares its numerator with incident frequency (bounded by sensitivity analysis)
- Demonstration set, not a portfolio ranking; the contribution is the **instrument and its evaluation logic**
</div>
</div>

::: notes
5:15–6:15. Say the right column unprompted; every point here is a question the examiner would otherwise ask. The framing to land: n=6 was a completeness criterion, and the small-n consequence is dealt with statistically on the next slides (exact permutation p-values, effect-size reading).
:::

## Evaluation: five strands, no single point of trust

<span class="tag">EVALUATION · CHAPTER 5</span>

<div class="cols3" style="margin-top:0.4em">
<div class="card"><h3>Stability</h3><p>Weight & temporal variation, Kendall's τ, exact p over 720 permutations</p><span class="verdict">τ = 0.60–1.00</span></div>
<div class="card"><h3>Weight space</h3><p>20,000 Dirichlet-sampled weightings, rank-acceptability analysis</p><span class="verdict">extremes robust</span></div>
<div class="card"><h3>Convergent</h3><p>Re-ranked with SAW & VIKOR</p><span class="verdict">τ = 0.73–1.00</span></div>
<div class="card"><h3>Discriminant</h3><p>Against incident-only baseline</p><span class="verdict">τ = 0.60 / 0.20</span></div>
<div class="card hot"><h3>Structural</h3><p>Leave-one-out rank reversal; absolute-mode variant</p><span class="verdict">reversal-free by construction</span></div>
</div>

<div class="takeaway">No external ground truth exists for non-code debt, so validity is triangulated: the evaluation establishes robustness, method-independence and discriminant value, and explicitly does not claim criterion validity.</div>

::: notes
7:15–8:15. This slide is the evaluation architecture. Say the takeaway line verbatim: it is the answer to the biggest examiner question (circularity / no ground truth) before it is asked, and the next slides unpack the three most interesting strands.
:::

## Robust where it matters

<span class="tag">RQ3 · STABILITY</span>

<div class="cols">
<div>
**Discrete configurations**

- Weight sensitivity 2025: <span class="n">τ = 1.000</span> (identical order)
- Weight sensitivity 2024: <span class="n">τ = 0.600</span> (middle of the field reorders)
- Temporal 2025 vs 2024: <span class="n">τ = 0.600 / 0.467</span>, tracking real profile change, above all SVC-01's shift
- The lowest-priority position is **identical in every run**
</div>
<div>
**Full weight space, 20,000 draws**

<div class="big">98.1<span class="unit">%</span></div>
<p class="small">of all admissible weightings place SVC-03 last, and rank 1 falls to SVC-01, SVC-06 or SVC-04 in every single draw (46%, 27%, 27%). The bottom is weight-independent; the single top rank is a property of the cluster.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="takeaway">Cross-year movement is read as descriptive context, not a quality criterion: services genuinely evolve, and a faithful ranking should follow them.</div>

::: notes
8:15–9:15. RQ3 answered: stable at the extremes, sensitive in the middle, and the middle sensitivity is a property of the 2024 data (grouped profiles), not the method, as the flatter 2024 Monte Carlo confirms. The takeaway pre-empts "isn't temporal instability a flaw?".
:::

## Does it earn its complexity?

<span class="tag">DISCRIMINANT VALUE</span>

Against a ranking by incident frequency alone: <span class="n">τ = 0.467</span> (2025), <span class="n">τ = 0.333</span> (2024).

<div class="cols" style="margin-top:0.5em">
<div>
**SVC-01 rises, fourth to first**

Infrastructure lifecycle debt (<span class="n n-hot">2,565</span> unsupported component months, patch recency <span class="n">53.10</span>) is invisible to an incident count. This is precisely the signal the framework was built to surface.
</div>
<div>
**SVC-05 falls, third to fifth**

High incident volume (<span class="n">171</span>/yr) offset by full patch recency and zero unsupported components: noisy, but structurally sound.
</div>
</div>

<div class="takeaway">The divergence is not noise; it concentrates exactly where multi-criteria measurement should add information over a single signal [consistent with @albarakManagingTechnicalDebt2022].</div>

::: notes
9:15–10:00. Short slide, one idea: if the framework merely reproduced the incident count, it would be redundant. It does not, and the two services that move are the ones that should move. SVC-01 jumps three places on structural exposure alone.
:::

## Where the methods disagree, and why that is a finding

<span class="tag">CONVERGENT VALIDITY · §5.6</span>

In 2025 all methods agree exactly under equal weights, with SVC-01 first, and SVC-03 is last everywhere. In 2024 they agree on the top pair but **split on its order**.

| 2024, equal weights | TOPSIS classic | SAW · VIKOR |
|---|---|---|
| Top-ranked service | SVC-04 | SVC-06 |
| High-priority pair | SVC-04, SVC-06 | SVC-06, SVC-04 |
| Next pair (near-tie) | SVC-02, SVC-01 (ΔC\* = 0.005) | SVC-02, SVC-01 |
| Classic vs SAW / VIKOR | τ = 0.600 / 0.867 | |

**Mechanism:** all four scorers name SVC-04 and SVC-06 as the high-priority pair. TOPSIS leads with SVC-04, whose 574 incidents vector normalisation preserves; SAW and VIKOR lead with SVC-06, whose worst-in-portfolio change failure rate their linear and regret terms weight more heavily.

::: notes
10:00–11:15. In 2024 all methods agree SVC-04 and SVC-06 are the high-priority pair and split only on which leads. TOPSIS puts SVC-04 first because vector normalisation preserves its 574-incident magnitude; SAW and VIKOR put SVC-06 first because its worst-in-portfolio change failure rate drives their linear and regret terms. Beneath the pair, all methods place SVC-02 and SVC-01 at ranks three and four, only 0.005 apart. In 2025 everything agrees on SVC-01.
:::

## Division of labour, not a winner

<span class="tag">METHODOLOGICAL CONTRIBUTION</span>

<div class="cols">
<div>
**Standard TOPSIS + SAW/VIKOR**

- Primary prioritisation signal
- Triangulation, not a single number: methods agree on the high-priority pair and split only on its internal order
</div>
<div>
**Absolute-mode TOPSIS**

- Rank-reversal free **by construction**: every leave-one-out removal preserved, where the classic top rank flips [@garcia-cascalesRankReversalTOPSIS2012; @yangIngeniousSolutionRank2020]
- Scores comparable **across observation periods**, uniquely among the methods used
- Complementary perspective; also powers the Monte Carlo cleanly
</div>
</div>

<div class="takeaway">The single top rank is contested within the SVC-01, SVC-04, SVC-06 cluster across the weight space: a compensability judgement the framework informs but does not settle, and saying so is a feature.</div>

::: notes
11:15–12:00. This reframing, disagreement as diagnostic rather than failure, is the transferable design lesson beyond the case. The takeaway line doubles as the answer to "so which service is actually first?".
:::

## Anticipated questions

<span class="tag">Anticipated questions · 1 of 2</span>

<div class="qa"><div class="q">Only six services: what can that prove?</div>
<div class="a">The contribution is the instrument and evaluation logic, not a portfolio ranking. Selection was by data completeness; p-values are exact over all 720 permutations and read as effect sizes; portfolio-wide deployment is stated future work.</div></div>

<div class="qa"><div class="q">You built and evaluated on the same data. Circular?</div>
<div class="a">Declared openly: the evaluation establishes robustness, method-independence and discriminant value, not criterion validity, because no independent measure of non-code debt exists. External validation is the primary future-work avenue.</div></div>

<div class="qa"><div class="q">Are DORA metrics really debt proxies?</div>
<div class="a">Treated as the central testable hypothesis, never a premise. @forsgrenAccelerate2018 validate the metrics; @nordExamplesTechnicalDebts2021 ground the diagnostic reading; the rankings match literature-predicted profiles. Longitudinal tracking would move it from plausible to evidenced.</div></div>

::: notes
12:00–13:15. Deliver these deadpan; each answer is one breath. The move being made: every hard question already has a stated, chapter-referenced answer in the thesis (Chapters 3–6), so the defence is consistent with the document.
:::

## Anticipated questions, continued

<span class="tag">Anticipated questions · 2 of 2</span>

<div class="qa"><div class="q">Aren't the differential weights arbitrary?</div>
<div class="a">Yes, and they are declared as a practitioner assumption. That is why the evaluation does not depend on them: across 20,000 Dirichlet-sampled weightings the lowest priority holds in 98.1% of draws and rank 1 stays inside the same three-service cluster in all of them.</div></div>

<div class="qa"><div class="q">Could this be misused to judge teams?</div>
<div class="a">Governance scope was agreed with the Head of Trading IT at the outset: decision-support for portfolio conversations, not a binding instrument. High-debt profiles typically reflect historical design decisions, not current custodians [@ahmadTechnicalDebtNot2026]. No team, vendor or individual identifiers exist in the dataset.</div></div>

<div class="takeaway">The framework measures debt indirectly and expresses the result as a relative priority. "Measuring" in the title means a quantitative, reproducible ordering, not a claim to have quantified the debt itself.</div>

::: notes
13:15–14:00. The takeaway restates the scope sentence from Chapter 1 verbatim in spirit; ending the pre-emption block on it shows the claim discipline has been consistent from the first page to the last.
:::

## Contributions

<span class="tag">CHAPTER 6</span>

1. **First application** (to the best of current knowledge) of TOPSIS to live ITSM/CMDB records for TD prioritisation in financial trading IT, closing the gap @lenarduzziSystematicLiteratureReview2021 identify field-wide
2. An **operationally defined indicator set** with explicit literature mapping to debt dimensions, plus evidence of its behaviour under a four-strand evaluation
3. A **methodological finding of independent interest**: sample-relative and absolutely anchored methods respond differently to concentrated debt profiles, consequential for the top of a ranking

**Practically:** a portfolio-wide, auditable priority ordering from data organisations already hold, surfacing exactly the debt current governance misses.

::: notes
14:00–14:40. Three academic contributions, one practical. If pressed on novelty, the four-element combination from the gap table (Chapter 2) is the defensible claim: each element exists separately, no study combines them.
:::

## In one sentence

<span class="tag">CLOSE</span>

<div style="margin-top:1.2em; font-size:1.15em; line-height:1.5; max-width:92%">
The framework does not measure technical debt.<br>
It orders services by the **operational shadow debt casts**, and within stated limits it does so <span class="n">reproducibly</span>, <span class="n">defensibly</span> and in a form a <span class="n">regulated institution can act on</span>.
</div>
